3. The learned Munsif found that the entire suit land was sold in auction in the rent sale and the land lord auction purchased the jama; that Exbt. 2(a) (dated 15. 4.25) a mortgage bond shows that Dijabar Kapalic mortgaged the land of the Jama wherein it was stipulated that the lands would remain in possession of the mortgage till Chaitra 1349 B.S., as such, the land was sold in auction while it was in mortgage; and that Exbt. 1, the deed of settlement was executed by Solokmoni in favour of the plaintiffs when the lands were sold in auction. According to him Exbt. 4 (Notice by debt settlement Board) shows that Solokmoni filed D. S. Board Case No. 500 of 1946 for setting aside the rent Sale and got it set aside; that Exbt. 5, certified copy of delivery of possession in Rent Execution Case No. 853 of 1935 shows that Solokmoni got possession of the land through Court on 1.12.1950 and that Biswanath, the plaintiff No. 7, had been an agent of Solkhmoni in Debt Settlement Board Case and identified the suit land at the time of D.P. (delivery of possession). The learned Munsif further found that Exbt. No. 1, which was executed in 1943, if this would not be acted upon then plaintiff No. 7 would not take so much interest for setting aside the sale. 

 Mrs. Rabia Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent, has contended on the other hand that the main question involved in this case is one of possession and who grew the paddy, question of title has no bearing in the suit. According to her the ruling cited on behalf of the appellant are not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case. She submits that the finding of the trial Court that Solokmony got possession of the suit land with the help of plaintiff No. 7 on 1.12.1950 in that case how can she give possession to the plaintiff by Ext. 1 ? Finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs are in possession basing on Exbt, 1-4, is, therefore, contradictory. According to her the plaintiffs have failed to produce any rent receipts showing payment of rent of the suit land in the year 1364 B.S., the relevant year for which they had brought present suit for damages. The suit is nothing but a test suit without any title and possession and the lower appellate Court has rightly dismissed it on a proper assessment of the facts and circumstances of the case. The learned Advocate, in this connection, has referred to the rulings reported in AIR 1963 (S.C.) 302 (India) in the case of Bamachandra Ayyar and another Vs. Ramalingam Chettiar and another and 12 DLR (SC) 132 in the case of Abdul Mannan Shek and another Vs. Lal Mamud alias & ors. 

 14. It is very difficult to follow the reasoning of the learned Munsif. He says that Exbt. 5 shows that Solokmony got possession of the land through Court on 1-12-1950 still he comes to the finding that the landlords were never in possession of the suit land after auction purchase because the evidence of defence witness is contradictory and shaky. His finding that Exbts. A.B. and C are bogus is also abrupt. He also found that Sdlokmony did never possess the lands. If that be so it is difficult to understand how can she give settlement by Exbt. 1. Under these circumstances these documents of title are not worth consideration I find enough force in the argument advanced by the learned advocate appearing for the respondent that these documents are not relevant for the disposal of the Money Suit which is purely based on damages for cutting away paddy alleged to have been grown by the plaintiffs in the disputed land. The learned Advocate has further submitted that had it been found as a fact that the defendant had title in the land in dispute but the paddy was grown by the plaintiffs the defendants could never have escaped the liability for damages if they had cut the paddy illegally. That being so it is equally applicable to the case of the plaintiffs. Omission to make specific mention of the documents as contended by the learned Advocate for the appellant has not affected the case on merits.
